tagline: A cottonwood station and limestone barn outlast eighteen months of mail riders.
intro: The Pony Express Historic Byway links Hollenberg Station near Hanover with Troy over 122 miles of Kansas highways. US 36 carries the long stretch between Marysville and Fairview; east of Fairview, the route loops south through Horton before returning toward Troy. Kansas Tourism presents the historic byway as a way to trace the mail riders’ passage across the plains, with surviving stations and a museum among its stops.

The mail service used places already serving overland travelers. Gerat H. Hollenberg built his station in 1858 for Oregon and California Trail traffic; the Pony Express began using it in 1860. The service ended in October 1861 after only eighteen months. Hollenberg’s property later became a farmstead, which the state bought in 1941. The building has never been moved and retains its original dimensions. The Kansas Historical Society took over its maintenance and management in 1963.

For an eastbound drive, begin at Hollenberg Station, then head south toward US 36 and east to Marysville. Continue through Seneca toward Fairview, then turn south toward Horton. Beyond Horton, the route turns back through Everest, Denton and Bendena before rejoining US 36 toward Troy. The byway ends just east of Troy.

moments.title: Hollenberg Pony Express Station
moments.text: Four rooms for the family, one for a shop and one for a tavern: Hollenberg Station combined domestic life with the business of overland travel. Pony Express riders and other guests slept in the loft of the cottonwood-frame building. Gerat H. Hollenberg built the station in 1858 to serve the Oregon and California trails, two years before the Pony Express began using it. A stable and blacksmith’s shop accompanied it. The station itself has never been moved or changed in its dimensions, and the Kansas Historical Society operates it as a state historic site.
moments.notice: The station has a cottonwood frame, wooden shingles and a stone foundation.

moments.title: Marysville
moments.text: An 1859 limestone barn preserves Marysville’s Pony Express connection downtown. The town stood on several travel routes, including the Oregon Trail, the Overland Stage and the Otoe-Missouria Trail. Later, the Union Pacific Railroad became a major employer, but its tracks separated much of the community from downtown. The main line moved to a bypass south and west of town in 2006, with separate levels for trains and the US 36 and US 77 roads. The old Pony Express station remains downtown. The limestone home station remains on its original site, another surviving part of the town’s transport history.

moments.title: Seneca
moments.text: At Fourth and Main, the former Smith Hotel site marks Seneca’s place on the Pony Express route. The town grew along the wagon route from St. Joseph to Oregon and California, and its post office opened in November 1858. The hotel became the first Pony Express home station west of St. Joseph. The present museum is across from the hotel’s former location.
